title: Inside AutomationBench — How a Cross-App Tool-Call Benchmark Works (with a τ-bench comparison)

authoring_notes.purpose: Single-focus deep dive into Zapier's AutomationBench (github.com/zapier/AutomationBench, arXiv 2604.18934, CC BY 4.0): how the benchmark is built, how tasks are defined, how an agent is run against it, and how it is graded. Secondary thread throughout: a structural comparison with τ-bench / τ²-bench / τ³-bench so the learner can place AutomationBench in the agentic-eval landscape and reason about which benchmark measures what.
authoring_notes.framing: This is an EVALUATION/BENCHMARK-DESIGN course, not a model-training course. The unit of study is the harness and the task spec, not a model. Read pages should quote real code from the cloned repo (file:line) and real task/assertion JSON.
authoring_notes.why_this_learner: Learner is building a production sales-call agent (Lina TMR) and recently closed the llm-training synthetic track with two open weak links named explicitly: (1) sim-to-real transfer measurement and (2) end-model (trained-agent) evaluation. AutomationBench is a concrete, code-level case study of how a serious team builds a deterministic, reward-hackable-resistant agent benchmark with end-state grading and no LLM-judge — directly transferable to designing the learner's own agent eval. ch-10 makes that transfer explicit.
authoring_notes.structure: 10 chapters in 4 phases. landscape (1) -> internals (2..8) -> comparison (9) -> lab (10). Internals follow the execution path of one episode: architecture -> tool discovery -> execute/world -> task spec -> grading -> hardening -> metrics. The τ-bench contrast is raised in-line in the internals chapters and then consolidated and sharpened in ch-09.
authoring_notes.per_chapter_format: Each read.md quotes real code/JSON from wiki/raw-data/automation-bench/ (the cloned repo) with file:line references, extracts the chapter's core insight + a practitioner guideline, and cites the library excerpts via [[wikilinks]]. Chapters may emit companion HTML under ch-XX/figures/ for the episode-flow diagram, the BM25 retrieval explorer, the assertion-grading flow, and an AutomationBench-vs-τ-bench side-by-side.
authoring_notes.depth_target: Source-rich. Every mechanism claim should be backed by a quoted function or task/assertion JSON, not paraphrase. Reconcile the public-doc numbers (README/blog/paper) against the code when they disagree — the code is authoritative (e.g. toolset modes, max_turns, partial_credit-vs-pass).
authoring_notes.known_doc_vs_code_discrepancies: Public docs say '2 tools' / 'max 50 steps' / '~47 apps, ~500 endpoints' / '600 public tasks'. Code shows three toolset modes (zapier=2 meta-tools, limited_zapier=named per-task, api=3 REST tools), max_turns default 25 (system prompt mentions a 50-turn budget), 44 app-states in world.py (~47 incl. subpackages), and 606 public task dicts + 200 'simple' sanity tasks. Flag and resolve these in ch-02/ch-03/ch-05/ch-08.
authoring_notes.tau_bench_comparison_anchor: ch-09 is the comparison centerpiece, but the contrast is seeded earlier: no-user vs user-simulator (ch-02/ch-05), generic discovery vs fixed tools (ch-03), end-state assertions vs DB-state hash (ch-06), pass-rate+cost vs pass^k reliability (ch-08).

tracks.title: AutomationBench Internals (one episode, end to end)

chapters.title: The Agentic Tool-Call Benchmark Landscape
concepts: From single-turn function-calling (BFCL) to multi-step agentic eval: what 'tool-call benchmark' has come to mean and why the bar moved
The benchmark family map: BFCL, ToolBench / API-Bank, AppWorld, WebArena / Mind2Web, τ-bench / τ² / τ³ — what each holds fixed and what each measures
AutomationBench's three-part gap thesis: cross-application coordination + autonomous API discovery + policy adherence, combined in one task (paper Table 1)
'Outcomes, not output': end-state grading as a philosophy, and why a company with a 9,000-app catalog defines the benchmark this way
Why the field scores <20% here: difficulty by construction, and what a low ceiling tells you about a benchmark's headroom

chapters.title: Architecture Overview: WorldState, the Episode Loop, and Toolset Modes
concepts: Built on the `verifiers` library: AutomationBenchEnv subclasses vf.StatefulToolEnv (runner.py) — what the framework gives you and what AutomationBench adds
WorldState as ONE in-process Pydantic root model (schema/world.py): no HTTP server, no database, no subprocess — fully deterministic given an initial_state
The episode lifecycle: dataset row (prompt + info) -> setup_state -> tool-calling agent loop -> rubric grading -> export_results
The three toolset modes and what each ablates: `zapier` (2 meta-tools, discovery required), `limited_zapier` (named tools listed per-task), `api` (3 REST-shaped tools)
The `world` injection trick: tools take `world` as a hidden first arg stripped from the model-facing JSON schema (tool_wrapper.py args_to_skip)
Reconciling docs vs code: 'two tools' and 'max 50 steps' vs the actual mode set and max_turns default

chapters.title: Tool Discovery: Search + a From-Scratch BM25
concepts: search_tools(query, top_k) over a ToolRegistry of ~400 named tools — the agent must FIND the tool, not just call it (tools/zapier/meta.py)
A from-scratch BM25 (utils/bm25.py): k1=1.5, b=0.75, Robertson–Sparck-Jones IDF, a tokenizer that splits underscores so `gmail_send_email` -> [gmail, send, email]
What a search result exposes: name, docstring-minus-world, and the JSON parameter schema; top_k default 5 and the max_top_k cap
API mode discovery: api_search over a tab-separated endpoint index (tools/api/search.py), lazily rebuilt when schema files change
Token economy: _compress_meta_messages rewrites stale search results to '[Previously found: ...]' once execute is called — and why current-turn results are left intact
Why discovery is a first-class tested capability and how the limited_zapier mode isolates discovery cost from execution cost

chapters.title: Execute and the Simulated World
concepts: execute_tool(tool_name, arguments) -> ToolRegistry.execute: JSON-parse args, re-inject `world`, dispatch the real Python function (tools/zapier/meta.py)
API mode: api_fetch(method, url, params, body) -> _url_to_internal_path routing tables -> route_<app> handlers (tools/api/fetch.py); 404 on unknown URL
URL-hallucination tolerance: ~15 known model mistakes (e.g. slack.googleapis.com) normalized to the right router — a deliberate eval-robustness choice
App state as Pydantic with extra='forbid'; to_display_dict() omits None fields so the agent sees sparse, realistic records (schema/<app>.py)
Real-API fidelity in the simulation: pagination, required fields, common 4xx codes — enough friction to be realistic, none of the flakiness of a live API
Why in-process simulation (vs a live sandbox) is the design choice that buys determinism and <1% run variance

chapters.title: Task Anatomy and the Six Business Domains
concepts: On-disk layout: domains/<domain>/tasks.py constructor functions emit task dicts; example_id ranges per domain; 606 public tasks + a 200-task 'simple' sanity set
The task dict: prompt (system + user trigger), answer='' (unused), info.{zapier_tools allowlist, initial_state, assertions}
Annotated walkthrough of sales.multi_hop_lookup (example_id 501): one task that spans Salesforce + Google Drive + Google Sheets + Gmail
Cross-application coordination as the headline distinction: solving one task requires reading and writing across multiple independent app states
Policy-in-artifacts: the routing rules live inside a simulated inbox message / a spreadsheet row, NOT in the prompt — the agent must discover and apply them
Recency-based conflict resolution and other reasoning traps encoded directly in the seed data (vs τ-bench's separate policy wiki + user simulator)

chapters.title: The Grading Engine: End-State Assertions
concepts: AssertionRegistry: decorator-registered, per-app checkers with signature (world, assertion_dict) -> bool (rubric/registry.py)
Must-pass (positive) vs must-not-occur (@negative_assertion) assertions, quoted from real task JSON — the anti-'shotgun' design
Two scores from one rubric: partial_credit = passed/total (the RL reward signal, weight 1.0) vs task_completed_correctly = 1.0 iff partial_credit==1.0 (the binary pass-rate metric)

Free-assertion exclusion: assertions already satisfied in the initial_world earn no credit, but BREAKING a pre-passing guard still counts as failure; the `excluded:false` escape hatch for do-nothing tasks
No LLM-as-judge: grading is pure Python field comparison on Pydantic models — the determinism/cost/repro consequences
Contrast: AutomationBench end-state assertion rubric vs τ-bench final-database-state hash — both end-state, but rubric gives partial signal and explicit negative guards

chapters.title: Hardening: Noise, Decoys, and Reward-Hacking Defenses
concepts: Deterministic noise injection seeded by example_id (domains/<domain>/_noise.py): reproducible distractors added at dataset-construction time
ID-namespaced decoy pools (sales uses the 099 range, operations the 098 range) so noise can never collide with or contaminate task-critical records
Near-match entity traps quoted from the data: acme-corp.com vs acmecorp.com, Sara vs Sarah, same-initials/off-by-one-phone contacts
The compliance-hold trap: every noise contact carries a 'do not enroll — pending compliance review' description that punishes agents who act on all records
Scope-creep traps: the user instruction says 'also process severance' but the policy artifact says HR must NOT — instruction-following vs policy-following
Why hardening is the difference between measuring reasoning and measuring luck: anti-shotgun negative assertions + count-locks close the cheap exploits

chapters.title: Metrics, Cost, and Reproducibility
concepts: The official metric is binary pass-rate (no partial credit in the score), with partial_credit retained only for analysis and as an RL reward
Cost-per-task as a first-class second axis: token accumulation (usage.py), a pricing DB with model-name normalization and a 24h cache (pricing.py), CLI cost overrides
Reproducibility: deterministic in-process world + seeded noise -> run-to-run variance typically <1% (contrast τ-bench's high variance at n=115 requiring 10+ repeats)
The 'simple' domain as a harness-validity control: even Haiku ~97% there, so low main-benchmark scores reflect real difficulty, not a broken harness
Reading a run: export_results JSON, per-assertion pass/fail, the visualizer; what 'false confidence in incorrect tool calls' looks like in the trace
pass-rate+cost vs τ-bench's pass^k: measuring capability-at-a-price vs measuring reliability-across-k-trials — two different deployment questions

chapters.title: AutomationBench vs the τ-bench Family: A Structural Comparison
concepts: The core axis: workflow automation from a single trigger (no user) vs tool-agent-USER interaction across multi-turn dialogue with an LLM user simulator
Tooling: generic Search+Execute discovery over ~400 tools vs a fixed per-domain tool set handed to the agent up front
Policy & state: policy hidden in seed artifacts + cross-app end-state rubric vs a policy wiki + single-app final-database-state check
Metrics: pass-rate + cost vs pass^k reliability; τ²-bench dual-control (Dec-POMDP, telecom) and τ³-bench's 75+ task fixes and voice/RAG additions
What each tests that the other cannot: AB = cross-app discovery + policy adherence under noise; τ = information elicitation, user coordination, consistency over a conversation
Shared blind spot: the sim2real gap (LLM user simulators and synthetic worlds both diverge from production) — and how to choose a benchmark for a given agent (e.g. the learner's Lina TMR)

chapters.title: Lab: Run It, Extend It, Reuse It as an RL Environment
concepts: Run a real evaluation: `uv run` the CLI with --model/--toolset/--domain, watch an episode, open the visualizer, read the exported result
The extension surface: add a task (a tasks.py constructor + seeded initial_state), add an app (a Pydantic *State + tools + route handlers), add an assertion type (one registry-decorated function)
AutomationBench as a verifiers / Prime-Intellect Environments-Hub RL environment: partial_credit IS a dense reward — the eval doubles as a training environment

Designing your OWN agent benchmark from these principles: end-state assertions, negative guards, deterministic seeded noise, a sanity domain, cost-as-metric, no LLM-judge where a programmatic check exists
Transfer to the learner's project: turning the Lina TMR sim into a graded, reward-hackable-resistant environment (the parked sim-to-real / end-model-eval problem from llm-training ch-29)
Deliverable: a short design memo — either a new AutomationBench task+rubric, or a spec for an end-state-graded benchmark of the learner's own agent
